analysis.time: Published on 2026-07-27. No specific event date reported in the evidence.
analysis.location_and_population: Not reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.event: Guidance on Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD), including symptoms, transmission, prevention, and vaccination information. No outbreak or event reported.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: No cases, deaths, or outbreak scale reported. HFMD primarily affects children aged 6 months to 5 years, with rare severe complications possible from Enterovirus A71 infection.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: No specific treatment available; management focuses on symptom relief. Prevention measures include handwashing, avoiding shared items, cleaning surfaces, and keeping sick children at home. A vaccine is available for EV-A71 in children aged 6 months to under 6 years.

analysis.brief_en: This article provides comprehensive guidance on Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD), a common childhood illness caused primarily by Coxsackievirus A6, A16, and Enterovirus A71. It details symptoms such as fever, mouth ulcers, and rashes on hands and feet, which typically resolve within 2-3 days. The disease spreads through direct contact with infected secretions or contaminated objects, with childcare facilities being high-risk environments. While most cases are mild, severe complications like brainstem encephalitis can occur. No specific antiviral treatment exists, so management focuses on symptom relief and hydration. Prevention emphasizes proper handwashing, avoiding shared items, and cleaning surfaces. A vaccine is available for EV-A71 in young children to reduce severe complications.

title: Sudden Arm or Leg Weakness in a Child Is an Emergency, and Late Summer Is When It Has Appeared Before - Medical Daily

analysis.time: Published Jul 30, 2026 12:00 PM EDT. Event timing: Late summer, with cases typically appearing after a respiratory illness or fever by a few days to a couple of weeks.
analysis.location_and_population: United States (49 states and the District of Columbia). Affected population: Previously healthy children.
analysis.event: Sudden arm or leg weakness in children, identified as acute flaccid myelitis (AFM), a rare neurologic condition. CDC guidance: Suspect AFM in any child with acute flaccid limb weakness, particularly after a recent febrile or respiratory illness.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Rare condition; peak years (2014, 2016, 2018) reported 120 to 238 cases annually. Can progress quickly to breathing difficulty requiring intensive care. Risk escalation signs include neck weakness, facial droop, difficulty swallowing, or breathing changes.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: CDC surveillance reports provide consistent guidance for clinicians. The frequency is reassuring, but the weakened link to enteroviruses is not established. Source limitation: Full original article body was reviewed.

analysis.brief_en: A rare but serious neurologic condition, acute flaccid myelitis (AFM), causes sudden limb weakness in children, typically following a respiratory illness. CDC urges parents and clinicians to recognize this as a medical emergency, especially when accompanied by symptoms like facial droop or breathing difficulties. While cases have been reported across the U.S., recent data shows lower frequency compared to previous peaks. The exact cause remains under investigation, though enteroviruses have been historically linked. Late summer is a critical period for vigilance, as this is when AFM cases have previously emerged.

CDC urges parents and clinicians to recognize this as a medical emergency, especially when accompanied by symptoms like facial droop or breathing difficulties. While cases have been reported across the U.S., recent data shows lower frequency compared to previous peaks. The exact cause remains under investigation, though enteroviruses have been historically linked. Late summer is a critical period for vigilance, as this is when AFM cases have previously emerged.

title: Probable Coxsackievirus Infection in an Immunocompetent Adult With Genital and Oral Ulcerations Mimicking Herpes Simplex Virus Infection and Behçet’s Disease - Cureus

analysis.time: Published on 2026-08-01. Event date: approximately one week prior to admission (patient presented with symptoms beginning about a week before admission).
analysis.location_and_population: Country not specified. Patient: 33-year-old immunocompetent woman with no significant past medical history, no immunosuppressive therapy, and no prior similar dermatologic episodes.
analysis.event: Probable Coxsackievirus infection in an immunocompetent adult presenting with severe vulvar ulcerations, oral ulcers, and a painful maculopapular rash on lower extremities that evolved into pustules, initially mimicking disseminated herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection and Behçet's disease. Reported in a Cureus medical case report.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Patient was afebrile and hemodynamically stable but demonstrated a marked systemic inflammatory response, including leukocytosis (white blood cell count: 21.3×10^9/L; 85% neutrophils) and elevated inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 42 mm/h; C-reactive protein: 15.4 mg/dL). Risk level not explicitly stated.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Patient received empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics and was transitioned to valacyclovir for suspected disseminated HSV infection; leukocytosis improved rapidly with persistently sterile cultures. Subsequent serologic testing demonstrated elevated Coxsackievirus A and B titers (≥1:100), supporting an enteroviral etiology, but limitations of serologic testing preclude definitive confirmation in the absence of paired titers or lesion-based PCR. Skin biopsy demonstrated nonspecific inflammatory changes with negative direct immunofluorescence.

analysis.brief_en: A 33-year-old immunocompetent woman presented with severe vulvar ulcerations, oral ulcers, and a pustular lower-extremity rash, initially concerning for disseminated herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection or Behçet's disease. Despite extensive testing, infectious and autoimmune evaluations were unrevealing, and cultures remained sterile. The patient received empiric therapy, and leukocytosis improved. Subsequent serologic testing showed elevated Coxsackievirus A and B titers, supporting a probable enteroviral etiology, though definitive confirmation was limited by testing methodology. This rare case highlights the diagnostic challenges of atypical adult Coxsackievirus presentations, which can mimic more common conditions, and underscores the importance of considering viral etiologies to avoid unnecessary antimicrobial exposure.
analysis.summary_en: A 33-year-old immunocompetent woman presented with severe vulvar ulcerations, oral ulcers, and a pustular lower-extremity rash, initially concerning for disseminated herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection or Behçet's disease. Despite extensive testing, infectious and autoimmune evaluations were unrevealing, and cultures remained sterile. The patient received empiric therapy, and leukocytosis improved. Subsequent serologic testing showed elevated Coxsackievirus A and B titers, supporting a probable enteroviral etiology, though definitive confirmation was limited by testing methodology. This rare case highlights the diagnostic challenges of atypical adult Coxsackievirus presentations, which can mimic more common conditions, and underscores the importance of considering viral etiologies to avoid unnecessary antimicrobial exposure.

title: CDC Publishes Six Years of Acute Flaccid Myelitis Data Ahead of the Condition's Late-Summer Window - inkl

analysis.time: Publication date: July 28, 2026. Event period: January 2020 to December 2025 (surveillance data). Seasonal window: August through October (late summer/early fall).
analysis.location_and_population: Affected population: Children (previously healthy, predominantly). Design population: Families with children.
analysis.event: CDC published six years of acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) surveillance data. AFM is a rare neurologic condition affecting the spinal cord's gray matter, confirmed through clinical symptoms, MRI, and laboratory testing. The report highlights a decline in cases (17-48 annually) compared to pre-2020 peaks (120-238) and notes an unexplained absence of AFM despite EV-D68 circulation in 2022, 2024, and 2025.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Cases: 17-48 annually (2020-2025), down from 120-238 in 2014, 2016, 2018. Deaths: Not reported. Exposures: Not specified. Risk: Low for individual families (fewer than 50 cases/year in ~73 million children). Surveillance gap: Only ~50% of AFM patients tested for poliovirus in stool specimens.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Investigation: Ongoing; CDC maintains AFM surveillance. Testing: Stool specimen collection recommended for all suspected AFM cases to detect potential polio. Prevention: Polio vaccination coverage (75-100% with 3+ doses) is reassuring; no specific EV-D68 vaccine. Uncertainty: Unexplained decline in AFM despite EV-D68 resurgence; no established reason for the break in biennial pattern. Source limitation: Full original article reviewed (content_status: full).

analysis.brief_en: The CDC has released six years of acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) surveillance data, revealing a significant decline in cases from pre-2020 peaks. Between 2020 and 2025, the U.S. recorded 17-48 AFM cases annually, down from 120-238 in 2014, 2016, and 2018. Notably, AFM cases remained low even when EV-D68, the virus most closely associated with AFM, circulated at elevated levels in 2022, 2024, and 2025. The report highlights a critical surveillance gap: only about half of AFM patients were tested for poliovirus in stool specimens, despite AFM being clinically indistinguishable from paralytic polio. The CDC recommends stool testing for all suspected AFM cases and emphasizes maintaining polio vaccination. The reasons for the recent decline in AFM cases remain unexplained, and officials continue to monitor the seasonal late-summer/early-fall window for potential changes in the pattern.

Notably, AFM cases remained low even when EV-D68, the virus most closely associated with AFM, circulated at elevated levels in 2022, 2024, and 2025. The report highlights a critical surveillance gap: only about half of AFM patients were tested for poliovirus in stool specimens, despite AFM being clinically indistinguishable from paralytic polio. title: Scientists recreate the 14 days intestinal infection behind hand, foot and mouth disease - isct.ac.jp

analysis.time: Published on July 28, 2026. The research recreated a 14-day intestinal infection period.
analysis.location_and_population: Institute of Science Tokyo (Science Tokyo). The study used a gut-on-a-chip model with human pluripotent stem cells to mimic the human intestine.
analysis.event: Scientists successfully recreated a 14-day intestinal infection caused by Enterovirus A71 (EV-A71) using a gut-on-a-chip model. The virus multiplied for 14 days without damaging intestinal cells, matching clinical observations in patients.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study focused on EV-A71, a virus causing hand, foot and mouth disease. No cases, deaths, or exposures were reported. The research provides insights into how the virus evades immune defenses and persists in the intestines.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The research team, led by Professor Kazuo Takayama, developed the gut-on-a-chip to overcome limitations of conventional cell lines. The model allows for more realistic evaluation of potential treatments. Currently, there are no approved treatments specifically for EV-A71 infection.

analysis.brief_en: Scientists at the Institute of Science Tokyo have successfully recreated a 14-day intestinal infection caused by Enterovirus A71 (EV-A71) using a gut-on-a-chip model. This breakthrough addresses a long-standing mystery: why patients rarely develop intestinal symptoms despite carrying the virus for weeks. The research revealed that EV-A71 multiplies in the intestines without damaging cells and evades the body's immune defenses by suppressing interferon responses. The gut-on-a-chip, developed from human pluripotent stem cells, provides a more realistic platform for testing new treatments, as conventional cell lines cannot sustain the long-term infection observed in patients. This advancement may help researchers understand how the virus spreads and develop better therapies for hand, foot and mouth disease.
analysis.summary_en: Scientists at the Institute of Science Tokyo have successfully recreated a 14-day intestinal infection caused by Enterovirus A71 (EV-A71) using a gut-on-a-chip model. This breakthrough addresses a long-standing mystery: why patients rarely develop intestinal symptoms despite carrying the virus for weeks. The research revealed that EV-A71 multiplies in the intestines without damaging cells and evades the body's immune defenses by suppressing interferon responses. The gut-on-a-chip, developed from human pluripotent stem cells, provides a more realistic platform for testing new treatments, as conventional cell lines cannot sustain the long-term infection observed in patients. This advancement may help researchers understand how the virus spreads and develop better therapies for hand, foot and mouth disease.

The research team, led by Professor Kazuo Takayama, aims to deepen understanding of the disease and explore how the virus spreads to other organs.

analysis.event: Official health advisory from Dalian CDC (Dalian Municipal Center for Disease Control and Prevention) highlighting disease prevention measures for August, including hand-foot-mouth disease, intestinal infectious diseases, foodborne illnesses, mosquito/tick bites, heatstroke, and drowning prevention.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: No specific case numbers reported. Risks include increased incidence of hand-foot-mouth disease (July-September peak), bacterial dysentery, infectious diarrhea, foodborne diseases (July-September peak), heat-related illnesses, and drowning incidents. Wild mushroom poisoning and jellyfish stings are also noted risks.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Preventive measures are provided, including vaccination for EV-A71, hygiene practices, environmental cleaning, food safety measures, mosquito/tick bite prevention, heatstroke precautions, and drowning prevention guidelines. No active outbreak investigation or response status mentioned. Source is a full original report.

analysis.brief_en: Dalian's CDC has issued an August disease prevention advisory highlighting multiple health risks during the hot, humid summer months. Key concerns include hand-foot-mouth disease (with EV-A71 vaccination recommended), intestinal infections, foodborne illnesses (especially wild mushroom poisoning), mosquito-borne diseases like dengue and chikungunya, tick-borne diseases, heatstroke, and drowning. The advisory provides detailed preventive measures for each risk, emphasizing hygiene, food safety, environmental management, and protection against extreme heat. Special attention is given to children, the elderly, and outdoor workers. No specific outbreak data is reported, but the document serves as a comprehensive public health guidance for the community.
